verdict.rationale: Keycloak's own docs give a complete self-hosting path: a one-line docker run of the official container image, an Operator install for Kubernetes/OpenShift, a guide for switching to a production database such as PostgreSQL, reverse-proxy, clustering and health-endpoint guides. Community users confirm running it self-hosted in production for years; reports of heavy memory use and difficult clustering are caveats, not contradictions. Missing for 10: explicit evidence in the pack that the core is openly licensed and free to self-host, and independent corroboration that clustered container deployments work smoothly.

support.subject: As an AI-native user, I can self-host the core product

citations.quote: Run Keycloak from a container image.
Switch to a production ready database such as PostgreSQL.
This command starts Keycloak exposed on the local port 8080 and creates an initial admin user with the username `admin` and password `admin`.
It's reliable, flexible and actively developed, so not a bad choice as a self-hosted IAM solution.
I've run keycloak securing internet facing apps with ~1000 users for years.
